selection_reason: There is no prior evidence yet, so the most informative first step is to establish a strong RNA-only baseline under the multiprofile setting and test whether a more expressive aggregator helps over simple avgpool. This experiment clarifies the value of transformer-based aggregation when multiple profiles per sample are available, while keeping the RNA encoder fixed (pca_n2000) to reduce confounding. It is a good use of limited budget because it probes a core architectural choice likely to matter for many later multimodal and RNA-only comparisons.

The only completed run shows reasonably strong performance for RNA-only PCA2000 with multiprofile and transformer aggregation, but it leaves two key uncertainties: whether the transformer is actually helping over a simpler aggregation, and whether the multiprofile setting itself is beneficial. config_002 tests the closest ablation of the successful setup by keeping RNA encoder and profile setting fixed while swapping transformer for avgpool. This is the best next experiment because it directly clarifies whether the observed result depends on the more complex aggregation, giving a high-value comparison under a limited budget without moving to a less relevant design space.

The current evidence is limited but clear enough to suggest that the RNA encoder and aggregation matter: pca_n2000 with avgpool outperformed transformer in the multiprofile setting, while we have not yet tested whether this holds for a stronger latent RNA representation. config_005 keeps the same promising multiprofile+avgpool setup and swaps in scvi_n200, which will clarify whether the gain is driven mainly by the aggregation choice or by a better RNA encoder. Under the limited budget, this is the best next experiment because it exploits the best-performing observed design while reducing an important uncertainty about encoder quality before moving to broader architectural changes.

Current evidence shows scvi_n200 outperforms pca_n2000 in the rna_only multiprofile setting (0.650 vs 0.591 accuracy), but we only tested avgpool so far and do not know whether that gain transfers to the transformer aggregator. This experiment tests the key open question of whether the stronger RNA encoder still helps under the alternative aggregation scheme, clarifying an important architecture choice while staying close to the best-performing direction. It is the best next use of budget because it exploits the promising scvi_n200 trend yet still reduces uncertainty about aggregation, which could materially affect performance.

Current evidence strongly favors scVI over PCA for RNA-only modeling, but it is still unclear whether the gain comes from the encoder itself or from the aggregation choice, since avgpool and transformer were nearly tied with scVI. This experiment tests scGPT under the same multiprofile RNA-only setup with avgpool, directly isolating whether a stronger RNA encoder can improve on the current best without changing too many other factors. It is the best next use of budget because it exploits the most promising direction (RNA-only, multiprofile) while still being informative about a key unresolved design choice: whether more expressive RNA representation can beat the scVI baseline.

Current evidence strongly favors scvi_n200 over pca_n2000 and suggests aggregation choice matters only modestly, but scgpt has only been tested once and performed poorly with avgpool, so its potential under a different aggregator is still uncertain. This experiment tests whether scgpt can recover with transformer aggregation in the same multiprofile RNA-only setting, clarifying whether the weak scgpt result is encoder-limited or architecture-limited. It is the best use of the next budgeted run because it directly probes a major unresolved design choice near the current best-performing RNA-only regime, rather than jumping to a more distant modality change with less informative comparison value.

The strongest evidence so far is within rna_only: scvi_n200 is clearly better than pca_n2000 or scgpt, and avgpool vs transformer is a small difference with transformer only slightly ahead. However, all completed runs use multiprofile, so there is still major uncertainty about whether the profile aggregation setup is helping or hurting. config_011 tests image_only with resnet50 on multiprofile, which will clarify the standalone value of image features and provide a clean baseline for later multimodal comparisons. This is the best next experiment because it explores a fundamentally different modality while keeping the design simple enough to reduce uncertainty efficiently under the limited budget.

The strongest current evidence is that RNA-only models with scvi_n200 outperform pca_n2000 and scgpt, while the best observed setting so far is scvi_n200 with multiprofile + transformer/avgpool. However, we have not yet isolated whether the multiprofile benefit comes from the profile representation itself or from the aggregation mechanism. This experiment tests the same high-performing RNA encoder (scvi_n200) in the simpler singleprofile setting, which will clarify how much performance depends on profile handling versus encoder choice. Given the limited budget, it is a high-value diagnostic experiment because it directly reduces uncertainty about a major design decision while staying close to the current best-performing direction.

Evidence so far suggests scvi_n200 is clearly stronger than pca_n2000 and scgpt for RNA-only, but the best aggregation choice is still only weakly resolved (transformer vs avgpool are nearly tied). This experiment adds the image modality to the strongest RNA backbone in a multiprofile multimodal setup, while testing weighted fusion, which directly clarifies whether the modest gain from images is best leveraged with learned modality weighting rather than simple concatenation/pooled fusion. Given the limited budget, it is the most informative next step because it exploits the strongest current direction while isolating a high-value design choice that could materially improve over the best RNA-only result.

The strongest results so far come from RNA-only scVI_n200 with transformer/avgpool being nearly tied, and the best multimodal result is already competitive but uses a weaker RNA encoder (pca_n2000) with weighted fusion. This experiment tests whether keeping the strong multimodal setup while switching to the better-performing transformer aggregation and weighted fusion can unlock additional gains. It is the best next use of budget because it directly exploits the best available multimodal evidence while isolating an important unresolved choice about how to combine modalities.

There is no prior evidence yet, so the main uncertainty is which broad modeling direction and architectural choice will matter most. This experiment tests a multimodal model with a strong baseline RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and image encoder (resnet50), using multiprofile inputs with transformer aggregation and concat fusion. It is a good first choice because it is both a competitive exploitation candidate for a likely powerful multimodal setup and informative for learning whether richer aggregation helps versus simpler pooling, while keeping the configuration grounded in standard encoders.

Current evidence is very sparse: we have only one multimodal result, and it used resnet50 with concat under transformer aggregation, so we cannot tell whether the strongest lever is image backbone, aggregation, or fusion. This experiment keeps the same RNA setup and multimodal setting but switches to the stronger image backbone candidate (imagenet_vit_l) while also testing transformer aggregation with weighted fusion, which is a logical extension of the only observed multimodal direction. It is the best next use of budget because it most efficiently probes a promising, high-impact design choice while remaining close enough to the current best-known configuration to exploit prior signal.

The current evidence is sparse but suggests the multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 setup is promising, and the best result so far used transformer aggregation with weighted fusion on a stronger image encoder. What remains uncertain is whether the resnet50 image branch can match or whether the gain came from the image encoder. This experiment keeps the promising transformer+weighted multimodal design fixed while swapping only the image encoder back to resnet50, clarifying the contribution of the image representation under a strong fusion scheme. It is the best next use of budget because it directly tests the key unresolved design choice with minimal confounding, while staying close to the current top-performing configuration.

The strongest evidence so far is that multimodal with weighted fusion is better than concat on the same RNA+ResNet50/transformer setup (config_021 vs config_020), and the best current result uses a stronger image encoder (config_027). What remains uncertain is whether that gain comes mainly from the image encoder or from the fusion design, since we have not yet tested the same transformer/weighted idea with ViT. Config_026 directly tests that extension by keeping the promising RNA encoder and transformer aggregation while swapping in imagenet_vit_l and concat fusion, which makes it highly informative for isolating the image-encoder effect. Under the limited budget, it is the best next experiment because it exploits the best-performing direction discovered so far while reducing uncertainty about the most important unresolved design choice.

Existing evidence suggests the strongest current direction is multimodal with the larger image backbone (imagenet_vit_l) and transformer aggregation, since config_026 achieved the best accuracy so far and config_027 also performed well. However, the effect of fusion is still uncertain: weighted helped in the resnet50 setting, but concat was better with ViT in the multiprofile transformer setting. This experiment tests the analogous high-capacity scgpt + ViT + transformer + concat variant, clarifying whether a stronger RNA encoder can improve on the best observed multimodal pattern. It is the best next use of budget because it directly exploits the most promising multimodal/image-encoder/aggregation direction while probing a major remaining design choice that could still move accuracy meaningfully.

The strongest results so far come from multimodal multiprofile models with pca_n2000 plus imagenet_vit_l, and transformer aggregation appears better than avgpool when using the same backbone. However, the fusion choice is still weakly resolved: weighted fusion beat concat with resnet50, while concat beat weighted with vit_l in the tested avgpool setting, so there is uncertainty about whether weighted fusion can help under the best-performing transformer+vit_l setup. This experiment directly tests that logical extension of the current best direction, using the promising image encoder and aggregation while isolating the remaining fusion decision, making it the most informative next step under the limited budget.

Current evidence suggests multimodal models with pca_n2000 RNA and imagenet_vit_l image features are strongest so far, and concat slightly outperformed weighted in the best transformer setting (config_026 vs config_027). However, aggregation is still an important uncertainty because only the transformer aggregator has been tested with this encoder pair. config_024 tests whether the better-performing image/RNA pairing also benefits from avgpool aggregation, directly clarifying whether transformer aggregation is actually needed. This is a good use of the next experiment because it probes a high-value design choice near the current best configuration rather than exploring a weaker branch.

Existing results strongly favor multimodal models with pca_n2000 RNA and imagenet_vit_l image features, and avgpool+concat with this backbone is already the best observed setting (config_024, 0.6287 acc, 0.5993 F1). The main uncertainty is whether the higher-performing image backbone can be improved further by changing the fusion rule while keeping the rest fixed. config_025 tests weighted fusion in the same strong avgpool/multiprofile/pca_n2000/vit_l regime, which is a logical extension that can reveal whether fusion weighting adds value or whether concat is already optimal. This is the best next use of budget because it directly probes a high-potential local improvement around the current top configuration, while still being informative about the importance of fusion choice under the strongest backbone settings.

The strongest evidence so far is that multimodal models with pca_n2000 and imagenet_vit_l perform best, and avgpool clearly beats transformer for this setup; however, we still do not know whether the image-only branch itself is doing most of the work or whether multimodal fusion adds value. This experiment tests the best image encoder (imagenet_vit_l) in an image-only, multiprofile setting with transformer aggregation, which should clarify the marginal contribution of RNA and whether the gain from multimodal models is real or mostly due to the image pathway. It is the best use of the next experiment because it directly resolves an important uncertainty while still probing a configuration that could plausibly be competitive if images dominate.

Existing evidence strongly favors the imagenet_vit_l image encoder over resnet50, and weighted fusion was slightly better than concat in the same multimodal setting. The main remaining uncertainty is whether the strong avgpool result with pca_n2000 generalizes to other RNA encoders, especially scvi_n200, while keeping the best-performing image backbone. This experiment tests that by swapping only the RNA encoder in the currently best-looking multimodal recipe (multiprofile + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted), which is a high-value next step because it both exploits the best-known design direction and isolates whether RNA representation quality is a major driver of the gains under limited budget.

Under a limited budget, it is a good first choice because it explores a key architectural decision likely to matter before spending experiments on more complex multimodal fusion.

It is the best next use of budget because it is a clean, informative ablation that reduces uncertainty before moving to larger changes like different encoders or multimodal models.
